claims.text: The alloy composition is Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
The alloy is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Stability of the high-temperature BCC phase is governed by an Al-induced thermodynamic driving force for local ordering.
The thermodynamic tendency toward local ordering is realized only when atomic diffusion is sufficiently activated.
Rapid cooling limits atomic mobility.
Limited atomic mobility during rapid cooling suppresses ordering and phase transformation.
Slow cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility for Al-promoted local chemical ordering.
Al-promoted local chemical ordering lowers the free energy of the alloy.
Local ordering triggers transformation from BCC to a more ordered low-temperature phase.
The proposed structural mediator is Al segregation coupled to the diffusion rates of transition metals.
Al lowers the mixing enthalpy in its local environment.
Transformation out of the high-temperature BCC phase is kinetically limited by slow diffusion of key elements such as Cr and Ni.
Rapidly quenched samples will largely retain the high-temperature BCC structure.
Slow-cooled samples will develop ordered-phase peaks detectable by X-ray diffraction.
Slow-cooled samples will develop nanoscale compositional variations detectable by atom-probe tomography.
Multicomponent complexity restricts atomic mobility at moderate temperatures in this alloy.
At sufficiently high temperature, complete equilibration can prevent the proposed kinetically limited mechanism from operating as described.
At sufficiently low temperature, transformation kinetics are too suppressed for the proposed mechanism to operate as described.
The fast-quenched condition serves as the experimental baseline against which slow-cooled samples are compared.

Failure of slow cooling to increase ordering or transformation relative to the fast-quenched baseline, or failure of transformation to correlate with increased atomic mobility, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
